fixes.explanation: Greater, friend. The verse says, “So Manasseh led the people of Judah and Jerusalem astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.” That's a heavy line, and the text says it plainly. I think this one hurts.

Twelve it is, friend. Manasseh, Hezekiah's son, is twelve years old when he becomes king, and he reigns in Jerusalem fifty-five years. TWELVE! Some folks can't be trusted with a kitchen timer, and this young man gets a whole kingdom.

Fifty-five years, friend! He reigns in Jerusalem longer than anyone would guess from a twelve-year-old with a crown. His father Hezekiah, the king before him, reigned twenty-nine years (2 Chronicles 32:33; 29:1). So Manasseh nearly doubles his father's run. That's a lot of mornings on one throne.

True, friend. The verse says he raised up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles, along with rebuilding the high places. Verse 2 says he followed the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. Manasseh is stacking one wrong thing on top of another.

Careful, friend, this one is True. Manasseh raised up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles, and that's on top of rebuilding the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down. So the statement holds up. He's putting back what his father took down.

Both courtyards, friend. The verse says, “In both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven.” That means these altars sit right inside the LORD's house, in two places. So they aren't in just one spot.

A bigger temple isn't in the deal, friend. God told David, Israel's king, and his son Solomon that He would never again cause the Israelites to leave the land, if only they were careful to do all He commanded through Moses. The condition is about doing what He said. Nothing in the verse asks for a grander building.
Nineveh fits an Assyrian king, so I get the guess, friend (2 Kings 19:36). But the verse says they took Manasseh to Babylon. That's the one city this verse names.
Careful, friend, this one is True. Manasseh prays, and the verse says, “the LORD received his plea and heard his petition.” After the chapter we just read, I think that's the plot twist. God listens.
Nineveh isn't a place this passage names for this part, friend. The verse says the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem and to his kingdom. That's where he reigned in verse 1. So it's a trip home.

This one is False, friend. The verse says Manasseh removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, along with the altars he had built. Then he dumped them outside the city. Nothing in the verse sends them to his palace.

False is right, friend. Manasseh removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, along with the altars he built, and he dumped them outside the city. Nothing goes to his palace. He cleans house.

The host of heaven comes up earlier in this chapter, friend (verses 3 and 5), but not in this verse. This verse says the people sacrificed at the high places, but only to the LORD their God. That's who the offerings go to.

Increases, friend. The verse says Amon did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done. Instead, he increased his guilt. His father humbled himself, and Amon went the other direction.
Confessing isn't the word this verse uses, friend. Manasseh humbled himself and prayed (verses 12 and 13), but Amon did not humble himself before the LORD. Instead, he increased his guilt.

Isaiah is a prophet, a man who speaks for God, friend (2 Kings 19:2), but he isn't named in this passage. The verse says the people of the land made Amon's son Josiah king in his place. The throne stays in the family.
Hilkiah is a priest, friend (2 Kings 22:4), and a priest isn't the one on the throne here. This passage never names him. The people of the land make Amon's son Josiah king in his place.
